reasons: Passages confirmed. Irish (Longes mac nUislenn; Windisch OCR 'hlechta' = 'blechta', confirmed by Hull edition unit G301020B:#1/8:3 and LL diplomatic G800011E:#1/8:32): every cow ('bó') and every beast ('míl') that heard the song yielded extra milk ('no-mbligtis', 'blechta'; bligid < *h2mlg-), so 'míl' here plausibly denotes milch stock. Etymology sound: 'bó' = 'βοῦς' (*gʷōu-); 'míl' < PCelt *mīlo- < *meh1lo- 'small animal' (Matasović s.v. *mīlo-, cogn. 'μῆλον'); no qualification field present. Two exact cognates coordinated as a livestock pair in a pastoral context; the Greek pair 'μῆλα' + 'βοῦς' is formulaic (Il. 18.524, 23.166, Op. 795; Fr. 180.9 with 'βοῶν' ... 'μήλων'). Against: a cattle-and-small-stock merism is natural in any herding culture and both nouns are the basic livestock words, so co-occurrence is expected; Irish uses distributive 'cech' with singulars, order reversed, and Irish 'míl' generally means 'animal'; the next sentence continues with every person ('duine'), so the Irish is a sweep over all hearers rather than a fixed herd merism. Single Irish attestation (one saga and its copies), no third branch. No derivation risk.

reasons: Passages confirmed. Homer: verse-end formula 'λίπε' + 'ὀστέα' + 'θυμός' (Il. 16.743, 12.386, Od. 3.455; Od. 11.221 with 'λίπῃ'). Lucretius 3.123 'deserit' ... 'uenas' ... 'ossa' 'relinquit': the claim misdescribes the subject; grammatically it is 'uita' (3.120), with heat ('caloris') and air ('aer') escaping in the cum-clause (3.121-122), so 'life leaves the bones' actually fits Homeric 'θυμός' closely. Etymology sound: 'λείπω' = 'linquo' (*leikʷ-, Latin nasal present), 'ὀστέα' = 'ossa' (*h3esth1-), both neut. acc. pl.; subject not cognate (renewal). Against: (1) independence: Lucretius was steeped in Homer and Ennius, and this is a didactic restatement of the famous Homeric death formula, so literary imitation of Greek is a real alternative to inheritance; (2) 'life/soul leaves the body/bones' is a near-universal death image; Latin pairs 'ossa' with 'uenas' and doubles the verb ('deserit'), not a formulaic match. Two branches only, one possibly derivative.

Passages confirmed. Irish (TBC LL, Cú Chulainn's lament for Fer Diad, G301035:#1/29/t#17:29-36): three hosts of the Táin fell by my hands, the pick ('formna') of cows, men and horses ('bó', 'fer', 'ech', gen. pl.), I slew them ('slaidius') on every side. Vedic AVŚ 12.2.29: fire in our horses, men, cattle, goats, sheep ('aśveṣu', 'vīreṣu', 'goṣv', 'aja', 'aviṣu', loc. pl.); 12.2.31 has 'puruṣebhyo', 'gobhyo', 'aśvebhyas'; AVŚ 1.16.9 'gām', 'aśvam', non-cognate 'pūruṣam' as objects of killing. Etymologies exact: 'bó' = 'go' (*gʷōu-), 'fer' = 'vīra' (*wiHro-), 'ech' = 'aśva' (*h1eḱwo-); no qualification field present. Against: these are the three most basic nouns for the living wealth of a pastoral warrior society; their joint listing is expected in a cattle-raid saga (the Táin is literally about cows, men and horses) and in Vedic protective charms, which enumerate livestock exhaustively (adding goats, sheep). Order, case, construction and predicate differ (Irish partitive gen. under 'formna' in a slaughter boast; Vedic loc./acc. in apotropaic formulas), and only one Vedic locus has cognate 'vīra'. Cognacy real, collocation not shown beyond co-listing; Irish is a late learned poem. Defensible as a low-confidence totality merism, not compelling.
